'''Multidimensional interpolation''' is the process of finding a multivariable function $f(x_1,\cdots,x_m)$ that for a definite set of datapoints $\{(x_{1,i},\cdots,x_{m,i},y_i)\mid i\in [0,n], i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ satisfies $f(x_{1,i},\cdots,x_{m,i})=y_i$.

== Grid interpolation ==

=== via Lagrange polynomial in multiple variables ===

If a "grid" of $n^m$ datapoints, i.e., values of $y$ at all possible combinations of $n$ particular values in each of the $m$ variables

$$
\{(x_{1,i_1},\cdots,x_{m,i_m},y_{i_1,\cdots,i_m})\mid i_1,\cdots,i_m \in [0,n-1],\, i_1,\cdots,i_m \in \mathbb{N}\}
$$

is known, then a multivariable-version of the Lagrange polynomial can be used to interpolate for $y$.

$$
P(x_1,\cdots,x_m)=\sum_{i_1=0}^{n-1}\cdots\sum_{i_m=0}^{n-1}y_{i_1,\cdots,i_m}\prod_{j=1}^{m}L^{(x_j)}_{i_j}(x_j),\qquad L^{(x_j)}_{i_j}(x_j)=\prod_{\substack{k=0\\k\neq i_j}}^{n-1}\frac{x_j-x_{j,k}}{x_{j,i_j}-x_{j,k}}
$$

which is a multi-variable polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ in each variable unique for each set of datapoints.

Similar to the [[Polynomial_interpolation#Lagrange_polynomial|one-dimensional Lagrange polynomial]]s,

$$
L^{(x_j)}_{i_j}(x_j)=
\begin{cases}
1, & x_j=x_{j,i_j},\\
0, & x_j=x_{j,i_k},\, i_k \in  [0,n-1],\, i_k \neq i_j,\, i_k \in \mathbb{N}
\end{cases}
$$

which guarantees that $P(x_1,\cdots,x_m)=y(x_1,\cdots,x_m)$ at all datapoints.<ref>{{#cite:Q2392}}</ref>

<blockquote>
$P(x_1,\cdots,x_m)$ is also known as the '''tensor product Lagrange interpolant'''.
</blockquote>

{{Hidden example}}
'''Surface temperature over a square of weather stations.''' 

Sixteen weather stations sitting in a $4^\circ \times 4^\circ$ grid measure surface temperature at various latitudes and longitudes.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Temperature ($^\circ$C) at each station
! latitude $\downarrow$ / longitude $\rightarrow$ !! $0^\circ$E !! $1^\circ$E !! $2^\circ$E !! $3^\circ$E
|-
! $50^\circ$N
| 22.8 || 23.6 || 24.9 || 26.1
|-
! $51^\circ$N
| 21.7 || 22.5 || 23.9 || 25.0
|-
! $52^\circ$N
| 20.1 || 20.9 || 22.3 || 23.5
|-
! $53^\circ$N
| 18.4 || 19.1 || 20.6 || 21.8
|}

What is the interpolated temperature at $51.6^\circ \textbf{N}, 1.4^\circ \textbf{E}$?

'''Algebraic solution''':

Let $x_1$ represent the latitude, $x_2$ represent the longitude, and denote the surface temperature reading at row $i_1$, column $i_2$ by $y_{i_1,i_2}$.

Then the interpolating multi-variable Lagrange polynomial is 
$$
P(x_1,x_2)=\sum_{i_1=1}^{4}\sum_{i_2=1}^{4}y_{i_1,i_2}\,L^{(x_1)}_{i_1}(x_1)\,L^{(x_2)}_{i_2}(x_2)
$$

where

$$
L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-51)(x_1-52)(x_1-53)}{(50-51)(50-52)(50-53)}=-\frac{1}{6}x_1^3+26x_1^2-\frac{8111}{6}x_1+23426,\\ 
L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-52)(x_1-53)}{(51-50)(51-52)(51-53)}=\frac{1}{2}x_1^3-\frac{155}{2}x_1^2+4003x_1-68900
$$

$$
L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-51)(x_1-53)}{(52-50)(52-51)(52-53)}=-\frac{1}{2}x_1^3+77x_1^2-\frac{7903}{2}x_1+67575,\\
L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-51)(x_1-52)}{(53-50)(53-51)(53-52)}=\frac{1}{6}x_1^3-\frac{51}{2}x_1^2+\frac{3901}{3}x_1-22100
$$

$$
L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)=\frac{(x_2-1)(x_2-2)(x_2-3)}{(0-1)(0-2)(0-3)}=-\frac{1}{6}x_2^3+x_2^2-\frac{11}{6}x_2+1,\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)=\frac{x_2(x_2-2)(x_2-3)}{(1-0)(1-2)(1-3)}=\frac{1}{2}x_2^3-\frac{5}{2}x_2^2+3x_2
$$

$$
L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)=\frac{x_2(x_2-1)(x_2-3)}{(2-0)(2-1)(2-3)}=-\frac{1}{2}x_2^3+2x_2^2-\frac{3}{2}x_2,\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)=\frac{x_2(x_2-1)(x_2-2)}{(3-0)(3-1)(3-2)}=\frac{1}{6}x_2^3-\frac{1}{2}x_2^2+\frac{1}{3}x_2
$$

Hence 

$$
P(x_1,x_2)=22.8\,L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)+23.6\,L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)+24.9\,L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)+26.1\,L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)
$$

$$
{}+21.7\,L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)+22.5\,L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)+23.9\,L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)+25.0\,L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)
$$

$$
{}+20.1\,L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)+20.9\,L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)+22.3\,L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)+23.5\,L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)
$$

$$
{}+18.4\,L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)+19.1\,L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)+20.6\,L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)+21.8\,L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)
$$

On simplification:

$$
P(x_1,x_2)=-\tfrac{1}{45}x_1^3x_2^3+\tfrac{11}{120}x_1^3x_2^2-\tfrac{31}{360}x_1^3x_2+\tfrac{1}{15}x_1^3+\tfrac{103}{30}x_1^2x_2^3-\tfrac{283}{20}x_1^2x_2^2+\tfrac{199}{15}x_1^2x_2-\tfrac{209}{20}x_1^2
$$

$$
{}-\tfrac{31823}{180}x_1x_2^3+\tfrac{87361}{120}x_1x_2^2-\tfrac{245249}{360}x_1x_2+\tfrac{32657}{60}x_1+\tfrac{45511}{15}x_2^3-\tfrac{62416}{5}x_2^2+\tfrac{174899}{15}x_2-\tfrac{93997}{10}
$$

Substitute in $x_1=51.6,x_2=1.4$,

$$
y(51.6,1.4)=P(51.6,1.4)=-\tfrac{1}{45}(51.6)^3(1.4)^3+\tfrac{11}{120}(51.6)^3(1.4)^2-\tfrac{31}{360}(51.6)^3(1.4)+\tfrac{1}{15}(51.6)^3
$$

$$
{}+\tfrac{103}{30}(51.6)^2(1.4)^3-\tfrac{283}{20}(51.6)^2(1.4)^2+\tfrac{199}{15}(51.6)^2(1.4)-\tfrac{209}{20}(51.6)^2
$$

$$
{}-\tfrac{31823}{180}(51.6)(1.4)^3+\tfrac{87361}{120}(51.6)(1.4)^2-\tfrac{245249}{360}(51.6)(1.4)+\tfrac{32657}{60}(51.6)
$$

$$
{}+\tfrac{45511}{15}(1.4)^3-\tfrac{62416}{5}(1.4)^2+\tfrac{174899}{15}(1.4)-\tfrac{93997}{10}=22.1162
$$

'''Numerical solution''':

<syntaxhighlight lang="python" copy>
import sympy as sp

x1, x2 = sp.symbols('x1 x2')

def lagrange_basis(nodes, x):
    """The Lagrange basis polynomials on `nodes`, from the product formula."""
    basis = []
    for i in nodes:
        p = sp.Integer(1)
        for k in nodes:
            if k != i:
                p *= (x - k) / (i - k)
        basis.append(sp.expand(p))
    return basis

latitude = [50, 51, 52, 53]                 # nodes of x1
longitude = [0, 1, 2, 3]                    # nodes of x2
L1 = lagrange_basis(latitude, x1)           # L^(x1)_1 .. L^(x1)_4
L2 = lagrange_basis(longitude, x2)          # L^(x2)_1 .. L^(x2)_4
print(L1)
print(L2)

temperature = [[22.8, 23.6, 24.9, 26.1],
               [21.7, 22.5, 23.9, 25.0],
               [20.1, 20.9, 22.3, 23.5],
               [18.4, 19.1, 20.6, 21.8]]    # row = latitude 50, 51, 52, 53; column = longitude 0, 1, 2, 3

# one term per station: reading times its x1 polynomial times its x2 polynomial
p = sp.expand(sum(sp.Rational(str(temperature[j][i])) * L1[j] * L2[i]
                  for j in range(4) for i in range(4)))
print(p)

value = p.subs({x1: sp.Rational('51.6'), x2: sp.Rational('1.4')})   # 51.6 N, 1.4 E
print(value)
print(float(value))
</syntaxhighlight>

'''Extra''': To plot the interpolating surface

<syntaxhighlight lang="python" copy>
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

latitude = np.array([50.0, 51.0, 52.0, 53.0])        # nodes of x1
longitude = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])           # nodes of x2
temperature = np.array([[22.8, 23.6, 24.9, 26.1],
                        [21.7, 22.5, 23.9, 25.0],
                        [20.1, 20.9, 22.3, 23.5],
                        [18.4, 19.1, 20.6, 21.8]])   # row = latitude, column = longitude

def L(nodes, x):
    """The Lagrange basis polynomials on `nodes`, evaluated at x."""
    return np.array([np.prod([(x - k) / (i - k) for k in nodes if k != i]) for i in nodes])

def p(x1, x2):
    """2-variable Lagrange polynomial"""
    return (temperature * np.outer(L(latitude, x1), L(longitude, x2))).sum()

lon_plot = np.linspace(0.0, 3.0, 121)
lat_plot = np.linspace(50.0, 53.0, 121)
surface = np.array([[p(x, y) for y in lon_plot] for x in lat_plot])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.0, 6.8))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
ax.set_box_aspect((1.35, 1.0, 0.62))
mesh_lon, mesh_lat = np.meshgrid(lon_plot, lat_plot)
surf = ax.plot_surface(mesh_lon, mesh_lat, surface, cmap="RdYlBu_r", linewidth=0,
                       antialiased=True, rstride=2, cstride=2, alpha=0.92)
ax.scatter(np.tile(longitude, 4), np.repeat(latitude, 4), temperature.ravel(),
           s=70, color="#c0392b", edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.9,
           depthshade=False, label="16 weather stations")
ax.scatter([1.4], [51.6], [p(51.6, 1.4)], s=170, color="black", marker="X",
           depthshade=False, label=r"query point (1.4$^\circ$E, 51.6$^\circ$N)")
ax.set_xlabel(r"longitude ($^\circ$E)", labelpad=10)
ax.set_ylabel(r"latitude ($^\circ$N)", labelpad=10)
ax.set_zlabel(r"temperature ($^\circ$C)", labelpad=8)
ax.set_xticks(longitude)
ax.set_yticks(latitude)
ax.set_zlim(16.5, 26.5)
ax.view_init(elev=34, azim=-56)
fig.colorbar(surf, shrink=0.55, pad=0.10, aspect=24,
             label=r"interpolated temperature ($^\circ$C)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
</syntaxhighlight>

[[File:Bicubic grid interpolation temperature.png|thumb|none|560px|alt=Three-dimensional plot of a gently curving temperature surface over a longitude-latitude grid, with the sixteen station readings marked as red dots and one query point marked with a cross|The interpolating surface through the sixteen station readings constructed via Lagrange polynomials in two variables. $1.4^\circ$E, $51.6^\circ$N is marked with a cross.]]

As observed, the surface is dominated by a plane tilted gently downwards from the south-east towards the north-west, predicting a gentle decrease in temperature along that direction.
{{End hidden}}

== Pointwise interpolation ==

Pointwise interpolation estimates the value of $y$ at one particular point, $y(x_1^*,\cdots,x_m^*)$, without constructing a general interpolating function.

=== via successive 1D interpolation in each variable ===

If a "grid" of $n^m$ datapoints, i.e., values of $y$ at all possible combinations of $n$ particular values in each of the $m$ variables

$$
\{(x_{1,i_1},\cdots,x_{m,i_m},y_{i_1,\cdots,i_m})\mid i_1,\cdots,i_m \in [0,n-1],\, i_1,\cdots,i_m \in \mathbb{N}\}
$$

is known, then first perform $n^{m-1}$ 1D interpolations in $x_1$, fixing $x_2,\cdots,x_m$ at all known values, obtaining $n^{m-1}$ interpolating functions $f^{(x_1)}_{i_2,i_3,\cdots,i_m}(x_1)$

Now evaluate each $f^{(x_1)}$ at $x_1=x_1^*$ to obtain $n^{m-1}$ interpolated datapoints

$$
\{(x_1^*,x_{2,i_2},\cdots,x_{m,i_m},y_{x_1^*,i_2,\cdots,i_m})\mid i_2,\cdots,i_m \in [0,n-1],\, i_2,\cdots,i_m \in \mathbb{N}\}
$$

Then perform $n^{m-2}$ 1D interpolations in $x_2$, fixing $x_3,\cdots,x_m$ at all known values, obtaining $n^{m-2}$ interpolating functions $f^{(x_2)}_{i_3,\cdots,i_m}(x_2)$

Now evaluate each $f^{(x_2)}$ at $x_2=x_2^*$ to obtain $n^{m-2}$ interpolated datapoints

$$
\{(x_1^*,x_2^*,x_{3,i_3}, \cdots,x_{m,i_m},y_{x_1^*,x_2^*,i_3,\cdots,i_m})\mid i_3,\cdots,i_m \in [0,n-1],\, i_3,\cdots,i_m \in \mathbb{N}\}
$$

Then perform $n^{m-3}$ 1D interpolations in $x_3$, $n^{m-4}$ 1D interpolations in $x_4$, $\ldots$, $n$ 1D interpolations in $x_{m-1}$, and finally $1$ 1D interpolation in $x_m$ to obtain one interpolating function $f^{(x_m)}$.

Then the estimate of $y$ at $(x_1^*,\cdots,x_m^*)$ is $f^{(x_m)}(x_m^*)$.<ref>{{#cite:Q2421}}</ref>

{{Hidden example}}
'''Surface temperature over a grid of weather stations (particular value by successive 1D interpolations)'''

Retake the same example as in [[#Grid interpolation]]:

Sixteen weather stations sitting in a $4^\circ \times 4^\circ$ grid measure surface temperature at various latitudes and longitudes.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Temperature ($^\circ$C) at each station
! latitude $\downarrow$ / longitude $\rightarrow$ !! $0^\circ$E !! $1^\circ$E !! $2^\circ$E !! $3^\circ$E
|-
! $50^\circ$N
| 22.8 || 23.6 || 24.9 || 26.1
|-
! $51^\circ$N
| 21.7 || 22.5 || 23.9 || 25.0
|-
! $52^\circ$N
| 20.1 || 20.9 || 22.3 || 23.5
|-
! $53^\circ$N
| 18.4 || 19.1 || 20.6 || 21.8
|}

What is the interpolated temperature at $51.6^\circ \textbf{N}, 1.4^\circ \textbf{E}$?

'''Algebraic solution''':

'''Step 1: interpolate in $x_1$ (latitude).''' Interpolate the four readings of different latitudes with the one-dimensional Lagrange polynomial at each of the four known longitudes, then evaluate the interpolating functions at $x_1^*=51.6$. The four Lagrange basis polynomials in $x_1$, built on the latitude nodes $50,51,52,53$, are the same at every longitude:

$$
L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-51)(x_1-52)(x_1-53)}{(50-51)(50-52)(50-53)},\qquad L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-52)(x_1-53)}{(51-50)(51-52)(51-53)}
$$

$$
L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-51)(x_1-53)}{(52-50)(52-51)(52-53)},\qquad L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-51)(x_1-52)}{(53-50)(53-51)(53-52)}
$$

so that, at $x_1^*=51.6$,

$$
L^{(x_1)}_{1}(51.6)=-0.056,\qquad L^{(x_1)}_{2}(51.6)=0.448,\qquad L^{(x_1)}_{3}(51.6)=0.672,\qquad L^{(x_1)}_{4}(51.6)=-0.064
$$

Hence the four interpolated readings

$$
y_{x_1^*,i_2}=\sum_{i_1=1}^{4}y_{i_1,i_2}\,L^{(x_1)}_{i_1}(51.6),\qquad i_2=1,2,3,4
$$

Substituting at each of the four longitudes, with the rows $i_1=1,2,3,4$ running from $50^\circ$N to $53^\circ$N:

$$
y_{x_1^*,1}=-0.056(22.8)+0.448(21.7)+0.672(20.1)-0.064(18.4)=20.7744,\\
y_{x_1^*,2}=-0.056(23.6)+0.448(22.5)+0.672(20.9)-0.064(19.1)=21.5808,\\
y_{x_1^*,3}=-0.056(24.9)+0.448(23.9)+0.672(22.3)-0.064(20.6)=22.9800,\\
y_{x_1^*,4}=-0.056(26.1)+0.448(25.0)+0.672(23.5)-0.064(21.8)=24.1352
$$

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Interpolated temperature ($^\circ$C) at $51.6^\circ$N
! longitude $x_{2,i_2}$ !! $0^\circ$E !! $1^\circ$E !! $2^\circ$E !! $3^\circ$E
|-
! $y_{x_1^*,i_2}$
| 20.7744 || 21.5808 || 22.9800 || 24.1352
|}

'''Step 2: interpolate in $x_2$ (longitude).''' Only one interpolation in $x_2$ is needed, since $m=2$: the four interpolated readings $y_{x_1^*,i_2}$ are interpolated along longitude with the one-dimensional Lagrange polynomial in $x_2$, giving the interpolating function $f^{(x_2)}(x_2)$, which is then evaluated at $x_2^*=1.4$. Its Lagrange basis polynomials, built on the longitude nodes $0,1,2,3$, are

$$
L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)=\frac{(x_2-1)(x_2-2)(x_2-3)}{(0-1)(0-2)(0-3)},\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)=\frac{x_2(x_2-2)(x_2-3)}{(1-0)(1-2)(1-3)}
$$

$$
L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)=\frac{x_2(x_2-1)(x_2-3)}{(2-0)(2-1)(2-3)},\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)=\frac{x_2(x_2-1)(x_2-2)}{(3-0)(3-1)(3-2)}
$$

so that, at $x_2^*=1.4$,

$$
L^{(x_2)}_{1}(1.4)=-0.064,\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{2}(1.4)=0.672,\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{3}(1.4)=0.448,\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{4}(1.4)=-0.056
$$

$$
y(51.6,1.4)=f^{(x_2)}(1.4)=\sum_{i_2=1}^{4}y_{x_1^*,i_2}\,L^{(x_2)}_{i_2}(1.4)=-0.064(20.7744)+0.672(21.5808)+0.448(22.9800)-0.056(24.1352)
$$

$$
{}=22.1162
$$

which agrees with the value obtained in [[#Grid interpolation]]
{{End hidden}}
